athlete_archetype.context: On the starting line; pre-race meal + bicarb load + caffeine dose taken; storm postpones race by 2 hours; nervous, never encountered before

question_summary: Athlete on the start line of the 20 km race walk with bicarb load + 200 mg caffeine already taken; race postponed 2 hours by electrical storm; should they top up caffeine and bicarb, and at what dose?
athlete_question_verbatim: Hey George, it's Max. This is crazy. I am on the starting line of the 20 km race walk at the World Championships. I had my usual pre-race meal (carbohydrate based, with a cup of coffee) two hours before the event, along with my sodium bicarbonate loading protocol. This is where I have 20 g of bicarb in capsules (~300 mg/kg) with 1600 ml of fluid to give me the benefits of a fluid load as well as extra buffering capacity for my race. Then I had a 200 mg dose of caffeine from gum while I was in the call room, waiting to move to the race start. However, an electrical storm has come through and the race has been postponed for 2 hours. What should I do? I'm feeling pretty nervous anyway because this is something I have never encountered before. Do I top up my caffeine and bicarb doses before I start? I usually take another 200 mg caffeine at the 15 km mark of the race but now I don't know if I will have too little or too much on board to execute my race depending on whether I take more now. How much should I use if I decide to top up?

louise_solo_answer.opening:
First — take a breath. You've found yourself in a unique situation that no study has ever had to consider, and given everything you've invested in your preparation, it's not surprising that you're feeling rattled. But you've done a smart thing in calling in some help.

Here's the reframe: everyone else on that start line is facing the same disruption. You can turn this from threat into opportunity by making a few sensible decisions and stepping back onto that line calm and confident. Let's work through it.
louise_solo_answer.fuelling_hydration: **Fuelling and hydration first** — the big-ticket items. Your pre-race meal has topped up muscle glycogen, and that isn't going anywhere in two hours. If you start feeling hungry or want a blood-glucose top-up, a small snack or a sports gel during your new warm-up is an easy fix. Your sodium hyperhydration is also still working for you — sip some fluid during the warm-up so you feel comfortable, and stay cool and shaded while you wait. These are easy adjustments.
louise_solo_answer.caffeine: **Caffeine — stick close to your original plan.** Your 200 mg dose is roughly 3 mg/kg, and the half-life of caffeine is 4–6 hours, so you'll still be feeling the benefits when the gun finally goes. I wouldn't load another full dose now — that risks pushing you into the wired, jittery zone on a start line where your nerves are already elevated. Keep your 15 km top-up as planned. If you want flexibility, caffeine gum is your friend — a smaller 50–100 mg top-up between now and the start, only if you feel you need it, gives you control without committing to a full second dose. The race will tell you.
louise_solo_answer.bicarb_in_line_wotc: **Bicarb — this is the question that deserves more thought.** Bicarb in endurance events is a newer area, with limited published research, so I want to bring in someone from our Wise Crowd who lives at the frontier of this work — a panel member who specialises in bicarb strategy in distance events. Their view: your blood bicarbonate is elevated right now from your 300 mg/kg load taken two hours ago, and it will stay elevated well into the new race window. The buffering capacity isn't depleted much by time sitting around — it's depleted by tactical surges and sustained high-intensity efforts. So don't top up. Adding more bicarb now risks GI distress on the start line, which is the last thing you want with two hours of nervous waiting ahead. Trust the load you've done.
louise_solo_answer.closing: **Closing thought.** Your competitors may not have prepared with your thoroughness, and most won't have expertise on hand to pivot smartly. You do. Instead of second-guessing your plan, settle into your focused race mode and execute it with the confidence it deserves. You've got this. One reminder before the gun — make sure your sports-science team and medical staff know the adjustments you're making, particularly if you decide to use any extra caffeine gum. And keep notes on how this feels through the race. You're your own best case study, and what you learn from today will sharpen every future race like it. It would be great to check in afterwards and reflect on how it played out. We all benefit from learning together.
